Lavoriamo da sessant'anni in una strada: We have worked for sixty years on a street with Rome's burial ground under its feet, along with the garden of Maecenas and the baths of Trajan. We had the story told to us, and we put it in order: 17 points, from the earthworks of the city wall to this morning's market.
Roma dipinta sulla parete della sala: il: Rome painted on the dining-room wall: the round temple of the Forum Boarium, the pines, and the panel with the poem in Roman dialect. This is not an old print — it is the wall of our own house.
: quelli che stanno fuori, oltre l'abita: : those who live outside, beyond the built-up city. The hill is born with the name of the people who live at its edges, and for twenty-five centuries it never quite stops resembling them.
Qui il colle è pianeggiante e indifeso:: Here the hill is flat and undefended: a wall is not enough. The Romans raise an enormous earthwork, the
, e ci appoggiano contro blocchi di tufo: , and set against it tufa blocks the size of a man.
Se ne vedono ancora i resti nel giardino: Its remains can still be seen in the gardens of piazza Vittorio and outside Termini station.
Fuori dalle mura l'Esquilino è il cimite: Outside the wall the Esquilino is Rome's burial ground: the common pits of the poor and of slaves, the
. Orazio lo racconta nella satira ottava: . Horace tells of it in the eighth satire of his first book.
«Qui stava la fossa comune della povera: “Here stood the common grave of the wretched poor.”
Mecenate, l'amico di Augusto, compra il: Maecenas, the friend of Augustus, buys the field of the dead and plants a garden over it. Rome's most infamous quarter becomes its most sought-after. Horace and Virgil walk in it.
L'Auditorium di Mecenate, in largo Leopa: The Auditorium of Maecenas, in largo Leopardi, came back to light in 1874: a sunken hall with a garden painted on its walls.
Il fuoco e la Domus Aurea: The fire and the Domus Aurea
Il grande incendio brucia Roma per nove: The great fire burns Rome for nine days. Nero takes the Oppian hill, a spur of the Esquilino, and builds the Domus Aurea on it.
Traiano interra la casa di Nerone e ci f: Trajan buries Nero's house and founds his baths on top of it. That is why the Domus Aurea has come down to us: it was buried, not demolished.
La vecchia Porta Esquilina delle mura vi: The old Porta Esquilina of the city wall is faced in travertine and dedicated to the emperor Gallienus. It is still there, wedged between two houses, on via di San Vito.
Papa Sisto III alza la basilica subito d: Pope Sixtus III raises the basilica right after the Council of Ephesus. The mosaics of the nave date from then: sixteen hundred years, never redone.
La leggenda della neve d'agosto — la Mad: The legend of the August snow — the Madonna tracing the outline of the church in snow — will arrive many centuries later.
Tagliati gli acquedotti durante la guerr: With the aqueducts cut during the Gothic war, the hills are left without water and empty out. Rome comes down to the Tiber and the Esquilino goes back to being countryside: vineyards and vegetable gardens for a thousand years, with the basilica in the middle like an island.
In Santa Maria Maggiore i marmorari roma: In Santa Maria Maggiore the Roman marble-workers inlay the floor: discs of porphyry and serpentine, ribbons of tesserae, rosettes. It is the pattern this site carries beneath its cover image and at the foot of every page.
I marmi li ricavavano dalle rovine antic: They took the marble from the ancient ruins: a hill that recycles itself.
Sisto V rimette l'acqua: Sixtus V brings the water back
In due anni papa Sisto V fa arrivare l'A: In two years Pope Sixtus V brings in the Acqua Felice, plants the obelisk behind the apse of the basilica, and has Domenico Fontana drive through the straight streets that still cut across the district today.
La sua villa, la Montalto, coprirà l'Esq: His villa, the Montalto, would cover the Esquilino until the nineteenth century: it was levelled to make room for Termini station.
Il marchese Palombara fa incidere sulla: The Marquis Palombara had a page of alchemical symbols carved on the door of his villa. The villa is gone; the door is not, in the gardens of piazza Vittorio. Nobody has ever fully deciphered it.
Roma diventa capitale e l'Esquilino si c: Rome becomes the capital and the Esquilino fills with apartment blocks in twenty years. Piazza Vittorio Emanuele II is laid out, with the longest arcades in the city, and with it our own street: via Principe Amedeo.
Ci arrivano tanti impiegati dal Piemonte: So many clerks arrive from Piedmont that the district takes its nickname from them.
Scavando in piazza Vittorio riaffiora un: Digging in piazza Vittorio brings up a brick ruin that Romans have always called the Trophies of Marius. It has nothing to do with Marius: it is a third-century nymphaeum. The marble trophies had already been carried off to the Capitol by Sixtus V.
Al numero 126 di via Principe Amedeo apr: At number 126 of via Principe Amedeo a family trattoria opens. A wooden door, a pale awning with the name on it, no illuminated sign. Sixty years later it is still there.
Il mercato lascia la piazza e entra sott: The market leaves the square and moves under the roof of a former barracks, between via Filippo Turati and our own street. Since then we have done our shopping two hundred metres from home.

Sui banchi il pecorino e il cardamomo st: On the stalls, pecorino and cardamom sit ten metres apart. We remain an orthodox Roman kitchen, but it is impossible to work here and learn nothing from the stall next door.
The district tells itself best at the table.
